prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

O zummer clote! when the brook’s a-glidèn So slow an’ smooth down his zedgy bed, Upon thy broad leaves so seäfe a-ridèn The water’s top wi’ thy yollow head, By alder sheädes, O, An’ bulrush beds, O, Thou then dost float, goolden zummer clote! The grey-bough’d withy’s a leänèn lowly Above the water thy leaves do hide; The bènden bulrush, a-swaÿèn slowly, Do skirt in zummer thy river’s zide; An’ perch in shoals, O, Do vill the holes, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Oh! when thy brook-drinkèn flow’r’s a-blowèn, The burnèn zummer’s a-zettèn in; The time o’ greenness, the time o’ mowèn, When in the häy-vield, wi’ zunburnt skin, The vo’k do drink, O, Upon the brink, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Wi’ eärms a-spreadèn, an’ cheäks a-blowèn, How proud wer I when I vu’st could swim Athirt the deep pleäce where thou bist growèn, Wi’ thy long more vrom the bottom dim; While cows, knee-high, O, In brook, wer nigh, O, Where thou dost float, goolden zummer clote! Ov all the brooks drough the meäds a-windèn, Ov all the meäds by a river’s brim, There’s nwone so feäir o’ my own heart’s vindèn As where the maïdens do zee thee zwim, An’ stan’ to teäke, O, Wi’ long-stemm’d reäke, O, Thy flow’r afloat, goolden zummer clote!

outputs.L2:
Golden summer water-lily,  
when the stream slips quietly and evenly  
along its sedge-lined channel,  
you ride securely on the surface,  
your yellow bloom held above your wide leaves.  
Past shadowy alders and stands of rushes,  
you drift upon the water.

A willow with ashen branches bends close,  
concealing your leaves beneath its drooping shape.  
All summer, pliant bulrushes sway gently  
along the riverbank,  
while shoals of perch crowd the deeper hollows  
near the place where you float.

When your water-drinking blossom opens,  
the fierce heat of summer has begun.  
It is the season of lush growth and haymaking,  
when sun-browned workers in the hayfield  
pause to drink beside the stream  
where your golden flower rests on the current.

I remember the pride I felt  
the first time I swam across the deep pool  
in which you grow.  
My arms stretched outward and my cheeks puffed  
as I passed above your long root,  
rising from the shadowy bottom.  
Nearby, cows stood knee-deep in the brook  
beside your floating bloom.

Of every stream winding through the meadows,  
and every meadow bordering a river,  
none seems lovelier to my heart  
than the place where young women watch you drift.  
Standing on the bank, they reach toward you  
with a long-handled rake,  
hoping to gather your golden flower from the water.
outputs.L3:
The golden summer flower floats serenely upon the smooth surface of the brook, sheltered by the cool shade of alder trees and surrounded by thick beds of bulrushes and drooping willow branches. Its bright blossom marks the arrival of high summer, when the fields are at their greenest, haymaking is underway, and tired workers rest beside the water after their labor.

The speaker remembers this place with particular pride and affection, for it was here, across the deepest part of the brook where the flowers grow, that they first learned to swim. The scene remains full of pastoral life: cows wade slowly through the shallows, while fish gather and dart beneath the clear water.

Of all the brooks, fields, and meadows the speaker has known, none is loved as deeply as this secluded place. It is made even more precious by the sight of maidens stepping into the brook to gather the beautiful, long-stemmed flowers that rise above the water.
outputs.L4:
The poem is a loving celebration of the golden summer water-lily and of the Dorset countryside in which it grows. Using rich Dorset-dialect words and vivid natural imagery, the speaker describes the brook as a lively, beautiful place filled with plants, birds, insects, and other wildlife. The water-lily stands out among these details, its bright colour glowing against the cool water and green vegetation. Through this careful description, the poet presents the flower not simply as part of the scenery, but as the crowning beauty of the summer landscape.

The poem also connects the natural world with rural work and community life. References to haymaking place the scene at the height of summer, when the fields are busy and the countryside is full of movement, warmth, and colour. The brook offers a contrast to the sunlit hayfields: it is a refreshing place of shade, flowing water, and abundant life. Nature and human activity exist in harmony, creating an idealized picture of traditional country life.

Alongside these observations, the speaker remembers swimming in the brook as a child. These recollections give the poem a deeply personal and nostalgic quality. The water-lily is associated not only with the beauty of the present scene but also with freedom, happiness, and youthful experience. Seeing or remembering the flower allows the speaker to return imaginatively to childhood and to a way of life that remains emotionally important.

The Dorset dialect strengthens this sense of belonging. Its local vocabulary and rhythms make the landscape feel distinctive and intimate, as though it can be fully understood only by someone rooted in the area. The poem therefore celebrates both nature and local identity. By the end, the golden water-lily has become a symbol of summer’s beauty, cherished memory, and attachment to home. Other places may have their own attractions, but for the speaker none can equal the brook and countryside of Dorset, whose beauty has been made uniquely precious by childhood experience and enduring affection.

**Upon the Path**

Upon the hill, beneath the silver moon,  
The wind whispered softly through ancient trees.  
“Thou art not lost,” it seemed to say,  
“For the road ahead is shaped by every step.”

The traveler raised his eyes to the stars and continued onward, carrying hope like a lantern through the darkness.

counterfactuals.output:
### The Water Crowfoot

O small-feac’d flow’r, that now dost bloom  
To stud wi’ white the shallow Frome,  
An’ leave the clote to spread his flow’r  
On darksome pools o’ stwoneless Stour,  
When sof’ly-rizèn aïrs do cool  
The water in the sheenèn pool,  
Thy beds o’ snow-white buds do gleam  
So feäir upon the sky-blue stream,  
As whitest clouds, a-hangèn high  
Avore the blueness o’ the sky.

counterfactuals.output:
### **The Golden Crowfoot**

Down-along where brook do bicker,  
By the mead an’ willow-tree,  
Golden crowfoot, glancin’ quicker,  
Rides the water wild an’ free.  

“Zee,” quoth Jan, “how bright her blossom  
Do lie ’pon the crystal tide—  
Like a little star from bosom  
O’ the heavens fallen wide.”  

Through the reeds the wind goes sighin’,  
Soft as mother’s even-song;  
Dumbledores be homeward flyin’,  
Shadows stretch the leas along.  

Still the brook, wi’ silver laughter,  
Bears each golden flower away;  
Yet another follows after,  
Fair as hope at break o’ day.  

“Ah,” saith Jan, “the Lord’s own pleasure  
Shines in lowly things, I trow;  
Kings mid seek for richer treasure—  
Give me crowfoot where streams do flow.”  

So when dusk the vale was filling,  
An’ the rook had sought his nest,  
Brook went under moonlight, trilling;  
Golden stars lay on his breast.
